title: Aperture latency-cost stitch — draft
content:
Purpose:
This note records an early experiment and narrative for what we’re calling the "aperture" pattern: gating context sent to the model (small prefix windows + opportunistic stitch) to trade latency for token-cost across sessionized workloads. It focuses on three practical operating modes we tested, with ascii charts and punchy takeaways for product collateral.

Quick summary:
- Aperture-stitched small-reqs: very low p50 latency, p99 depends heavily on KV cache hit and stitch overhead; per-query token cost rises if stitch frequency increases.
- Batch-aggregated background: highest cost efficiency (tokens amortized) but increased median latency and long tail for interactive requests.
- Hybrid prefetch + short-stitch: sweet spot for chat features where p95 is acceptable and cost is 20-40% lower than naive full-context calls.

Experiment matrix (config):
- Model: open-llama-13b-q4 (runtime profile: quantized float with kernel A)
- HW: 8xA100 equivalent pool (dedicated test pool)
- Workload: interactive chat sessions (avg turn tokens = 18, avg context growth per session = 320 tokens)
- Metrics: p50, p95, p99 latency (ms), tokens billed per session, effective cost-per-response (normalized)
- Aperture variants: 
  * A1: prefix-only (64 tokens) per-turn call, no stitching
  * A2: prefix + opportunistic stitch every 4 turns (stitch sends missing context incrementally)
  * B1: small-batch (groups of 8 turns, 250ms queuing)

Raw numbers (aggregated, median of 3 runs):
+-------------------------------+---------+---------+---------+-----------------+
| Mode                          | p50 ms  | p95 ms  | p99 ms  | tokens/session   |
+-------------------------------+---------+---------+---------+-----------------+
| Baseline full-context         | 210     | 410     | 740     | 1120            |
| A1 prefix-only (64)          | 38      | 210     | 980     | 620             |
| A2 prefix+stitch (q4)        | 52      | 190     | 420     | 740             |
| B1 small-batch (250ms)       | 180     | 360     | 620     | 420             |
+-------------------------------+---------+---------+---------+-----------------+
Notes on numbers:
- A1 gives great median latency (38ms) but suffers on p99 due to occasional long tail when a long stitch or reroute happens; token count reduced because we don't repeatedly send full context, but user-visible quality can drop if partial context misses critical info.
- A2 smooths the p99 by amortizing stitch costs and keeping token overhead modest. We saw ~20% higher tokens than A1 but p99 improved from 980ms -> 420ms.
- B1 (batching) is cheapest token-wise but adds 150ms median overhead and still has tails from batch assembly and slow slot allocation.

Small ascii visualization: relative latency stacks (normalized to baseline p50=1.0)
- baseline    : |====| median(1.0) p95(1.95) p99(3.52)
- prefix A1  : |-| median(0.18) p95(1.0) p99(4.6)
- stitch A2  : |--| median(0.25) p95(0.92) p99(2.0)
- batch B1   : |===| median(0.86) p95(1.71) p99(2.78)

Cost-per-session (normalized dollar units):
- baseline full-context: 1.00
- A1 prefix-only: 0.56
- A2 prefix+stitch: 0.68
- B1 small-batch: 0.37

Interpretation / qualitative findings:
- Stitching is effective if the stitching latency itself is controlled (small incremental updates, efficient KV delta). The point of diminishing returns is when stitch messages are >120 tokens per update (we saw p99 regressions).
- Batching remains the best pure-dollar option, but it requires product-level tolerance for median latency and queuing. For consumer chat flows (low friction) small ms of added latency are OK; for synchronous UI interactions (typeahead/autocomplete) they are not.
- Prefix-only (A1) is dangerous for task correctness where context evolution matters (multi-turn instructions), but cheap for single-turn Q/A or assistant hints.

Operational checklist (what to instrument):
- KV cache hit ratio per-session (slice by tenant tier)
- Stitch size distribution (tokens per stitch)
- Stitch latency percentile (p50/p95/p99) and dependent fallbacks (retries, fallback to full-context)
- Queueing delay histogram for batched lanes (ms bins 0-50-100-250-500)
- Token billing delta per-session vs baseline (weekly, by cohort)

Suggested product collateral angles:
1) "Tiny aperture": call out 2-3 short examples where 64-token prefix + periodic stitch reduces bill by ~40% for chat apps while keeping p95 < 200ms.
2) "Batch-for-nightly": show hybrid architectures where interactive lane uses aperture+stitch, background processes compact full-context for embeddings or analytics.
3) "Stitch reliability playbook": recommended knobs (stitch backoff, partial-merge heuristics, idempotent stitch ids) to avoid the long tails seen in A1.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Quant regimes: we ran on q4 profiles; need to re-run q5 and mixed precision to validate kernel switch cost (observed slight increase in stitch serialization with q5).
- Region routing: do stitch sizes amplify network egress costs for cross-region sessions? quick test needed.
- UX thresholds: run A/B with product to see how much p95 bump is tolerated before engagement drops (target cohorts: search assistant vs guided workflow).

Draft copy blurb for collateral (two-line):
"Aperture stitching lets you pay for the context you need, when you need it. By sending a small prefix for each turn and stitching only the deltas, teams can keep interactive latencies low and reduce tokens billed by up to ~40% compared to naive full-context calls — with modest engineering controls to avoid long-tail regressions."

Next steps (owners):
- Re-run q5 profile sweep (Rohit) — due 2028-11-14
- Lightweight integration test for cross-region stitch cost (Claire) — due 2028-11-17
- Draft collateral one-pager with three visuals stripped from the ascii tables (Sasha) — due 2028-11-09

Appendix: quick failure modes observed (notes to self) 
- Large-system GC spikes in test cluster caused stitch serialization timeouts; add jitter and retry.
- Some clients mis-ordered stitch fragments when network reordering occurred; require sequence ids and reassembly logic.
- Billing contortions: watch for double-billing when fallback full-context called after stitch timeout; instrument idempotency.

End of draft.

(Informal notes: this doc is meant for early internal review and sketches, not final benchmarking collateral. Keep language simple for design review.)
